purpose: Teaching checkpoints based on existing public educational stories; not new scientific discoveries

choices.text: Bacteria grew poorly near a patch of mold.
choices.feedback: That's an observation from the dish; it gives us a clue worth testing.

choices.text: The mold had already cured patients of infections.
choices.feedback: Not yet. A laboratory observation does not demonstrate a safe treatment in people.

penicillin.question: Which explanation would researchers need to test?

choices.text: The mold released something that affected nearby bacteria.
choices.feedback: A useful hypothesis. Investigators still had to test what caused the inhibition.

choices.text: All mold can kill all bacteria.
choices.feedback: The observation did not establish that. Different molds and bacteria can behave differently.

penicillin.question: What was missing before penicillin could become useful medicine?

choices.text: Purification, careful testing and reliable production.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Other researchers had to make and evaluate the substance as a treatment.

choices.text: Nothing; a clear area on a dish was enough.
choices.feedback: A petri dish cannot establish safety, dosage, effectiveness or production quality in people.

penicillin.question: Which lesson best fits the discovery?

choices.text: A verified small observation can start an important collaborative effort.
choices.feedback: Yes. The initial observation and later testing/production all mattered.

choices.text: One person found an instant, finished medical treatment.
choices.feedback: That leaves out years of essential teamwork, development and evaluation.

insulin.question: Why was the pancreas worth investigating?

choices.text: Researchers had connected the pancreas with diabetes and blood sugar control.
choices.feedback: Yes. That clue prompted experiments to identify a substance involved in regulating sugar.

choices.text: Researchers already knew every cause of diabetes.
choices.feedback: They did not. Scientific understanding was developing and multiple questions remained.

insulin.question: What did experiments using pancreatic extracts in animals provide?

choices.text: Promising experimental evidence to investigate further.
choices.feedback: Correct. Animal results can guide the next experiment, but do not by themselves prove human benefit.

choices.text: Proof that every person with diabetes could be treated safely.
choices.feedback: Animal findings were not enough for that conclusion.

choices.text: A better-prepared extract was an important step in successful human treatment.
choices.feedback: Yes. The first attempt was less successful; preparation and testing mattered.

choices.text: Purification proved all insulin preparations had the same effects.
choices.feedback: Different preparations and circumstances cannot be treated as identical without evidence.

insulin.question: What makes this a teamwork story?

choices.text: Experiments, chemical purification, clinical care and production all contributed.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Multiple complementary skills turned an idea into treatment.

choices.text: The first animal experiment made further work unnecessary.
choices.feedback: The human and production stages still demanded careful work.

braf-melanoma.question: What was the first major clue in the 2002 study?

choices.text: BRAF mutations were found in many of the melanoma samples studied.
choices.feedback: Yes. The paper reported BRAF mutations in 66% of malignant melanoma specimens in that study.

choices.text: BRAF mutations were found in every cancer.
choices.feedback: No. Frequencies varied across tumor types and samples.

braf-melanoma.question: What is a testable next hypothesis?

choices.text: Some tumors might depend on altered BRAF signaling and respond to targeted inhibition.
choices.feedback: That is a testable possibility—not yet a demonstrated clinical result.

choices.text: Every cancer with any BRAF variation must respond to the same drug.
choices.feedback: Mutations, tumor context and treatment responses differ. That claim is unsupported.

braf-melanoma.question: What did the 2011 randomized trial report?

choices.text: A higher confirmed response rate with vemurafenib than dacarbazine in the trial population.
choices.feedback: Yes. The study reported confirmed response rates of 48% and 5% in evaluable patients, with trial-specific eligibility.

choices.text: A permanent cure for all patients with melanoma.
choices.feedback: No. A response is not a cure; benefit and limitations depend on the population and follow-up.

braf-melanoma.question: Which scientific limit should we keep in mind?

choices.text: Original trial results must be interpreted in the studied population and historical context.
choices.feedback: Correct. Modern standards of care have evolved; the study is a discovery lesson, not treatment guidance.

choices.text: A study showing tumor shrinkage removes the need for safety or follow-up data.
choices.feedback: Safety, durability and long-term outcomes remain essential.
